lesson.menu_title: The Short Verbs That Run the Deal
lesson.menu_desc: Phrasal verbs as professional language: separable and inseparable, the pronoun in the middle, and the formal verb they replace in a meeting
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- The Short Verbs That Run the Deal
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 12 -- The Short Verbs That Run the Deal

vocab.title: Match each phrasal verb to its formal meaning
defs: to prepare a written document, such as a contract or a plan
to mention a subject so that people discuss it
to say no to an offer or a request
to fail before it is completed (a deal or a plan)
to investigate; to try to find out the facts
to decide that something is not possible or will not be considered
to do a task that was planned, such as an audit or a test
to suggest an idea or a plan so that others can consider it

paras: Dear Amanda, thank you for your time on Tuesday, and thank you for bringing up the exclusivity point so early in the call. It was the right moment to discuss it, and I want to set out where we are before the next draft.

First, we have looked into your concern about clause 7.2. My client understands that a full exclusivity period, with no end date, is difficult for a project at this stage. For that reason, we are not going to insist on the original wording.

Second, your commercial director put forward a compromise during the call: exclusivity for six months, and after that the right to offer any remaining credits to other buyers. My client has not turned it down. However, they cannot accept it until the verification body has carried out the site visit in May.

Third, I should be clear about one point. My client has ruled out any change to the fixed price. They have accepted the review clause, but the price itself is not open for discussion, and I would not like the deal to fall through over a point that is already closed.
As a next step, I will draw up a revised version of clause 7 and send it to you by Friday. If anything in this email does not match your notes, please let me know before then. Kind regards, Ingrid.
reading.source: Sample email written for this lesson. Nothing here is a real negotiation.

choices: To end the negotiation, because the two sides could not agree on the price.
To confirm what changed after the call, what is still open, what is closed, and what happens next.
To ask the seller to send a new draft of the whole agreement as soon as it is possible.

items: Amanda raised the exclusivity point late in the call.
Ingrid thanks her for bringing it up so early.
The buyer will not insist on exclusivity with no end date.
The second paragraph says they will not insist on the original wording.
The six-month compromise came from the buyer.
The seller's commercial director put it forward.
The buyer has already accepted the six-month compromise.
They have not turned it down, but they will wait for the site visit in May.
The fixed price is not open for discussion.
The client has ruled out any change to it.
Ingrid will prepare the revised clause herself.
She will draw up a revised version of clause 7 by Friday.

items.situation: Rafael asks: "Did the buyer accept our six-month idea?"
tips: Not yet. They have not turned it down, but they are waiting for the site visit.
turn down = reject; not yet, not no.

items.situation: He asks: "Who is writing the new clause?"
tips: Their counsel is drawing it up. We will have it by Friday.
draw it up: the pronoun goes in the middle.

items.situation: He asks: "Can we still change the price?"
tips: No. They have ruled it out.
rule it out, never rule out it.

items.situation: He asks: "What are you doing about the registry problem?"
tips: I am looking into it, and I will come back to you on Monday.
look into it: inseparable, the pronoun goes at the end.

items.situation: He asks: "When is the site visit?"
tips: The verification body will carry it out in May.
carry out a visit, carry it out.

items.situation: He asks: "What is the real risk now?"
tips: That the deal falls through over the price, which is already closed.

listenings.text: Amanda, it is Rafael. I spoke to the board this morning, and I want to give you the short version before the call with Ingrid. I brought up the six-month idea, and nobody turned it down, which is good news. But the chairman asked a question I could not answer: if the buyer backs out after the site visit, can we sell the credits to somebody else immediately, or do we have to wait? Could you look into that today? The board has also ruled out any discount on the price, so please do not put forward anything that sounds like one. And one more thing: the finance team wants to carry out its own review of the payment dates before we sign. I told them they would have your comments by Thursday. Call me if that is a problem.

A lot of lawyers believe that phrasal verbs are informal, so they avoid them. That is half true. In a contract, you will read that the parties shall conduct an audit, or that the buyer may reject an offer. But in the meeting about that contract, nobody talks like that. People say they will carry out the audit, look into the problem, or turn the offer down. If you only use the formal verbs, you sound like you are reading the agreement out loud. So you need both: the formal verb for the document, and the phrasal verb for the room. One more detail, and it is the one that gives non-native speakers away. With most of these verbs, a pronoun goes in the middle. You draw it up, you turn it down, you rule it out. Never draw up it. And with a few, like look into, the pronoun stays at the end: we are looking into it.

extra_audio.text: Open the call and say who you are. Then refer to the last meeting. Then go through the first update. Then go through the second update. Then put forward your recommendation. And finally, wrap up and agree the next step.
